Strait of Hormuz · Daily brief · UTC
10 October 2026 .
Brent $ 104.72 + 0.83 % · Transits 4 (2026-10-04) · AI-assisted
01 The Financial Times reports tanker attacks in the strait have surged to a wartime high and Iran has extended strikes beyond the strait into the Gulf.

02 The Maritime Executive reports the IRGC has expanded its threat against non-compliant vessels as more tankers are struck.

Situation
The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to normal commercial traffic, with the Financial Times reporting that tanker attacks have reached a wartime high and that Iran has extended strikes beyond the strait into the Gulf. The Maritime Executive reports the IRGC is broadening its threat posture against vessels it deems non-compliant, and The Maritime Executive further reports more tankers have been struck in this period. USNI News, citing the International Maritime Organization, reported that nine ships, mostly crude oil tankers, were struck in or near the strait between October 1 and that Tuesday, at a rate of nearly one per day. IMF PortWatch recorded 4 transits on October 4, against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day. A vessel was struck in the strait on October 9 and the Revolutionary Guard warned of punishment for route violations, per news.sbs.co.kr. NDTV reports an LPG tanker was struck in the strait, reported on October 9, with the Iranian Revolutionary Guard saying the vessel was taking an illegal route. Brent crude stood at $104.72 as of 06:21 UTC, a gain of 0.83% in the last session before the close; futures markets are shut and the price is unchanged since close. As of 06:20 UTC, 109 AIS-visible vessels were holding position away from berth in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf watch box, a count that leaves out ships within 25km of a working port. On the Hormuz Index, Crisis Pressure, the state composite, sits in the extreme band, with its value set by physical transit deviation alone; the Escalation Forecast sits in the high band, with the Brent-WTI forward spread as its top contributor.
